do: Don’t quit yet. For the next few days, use it the way you always do.
Allow it. No guilt, no promises. You’re studying it, not fighting it.
Write down what you think nicotine gives you: calm, focus, a break.
Each time, write one line: the time, where you are, what you wanted from it.
Ten minutes after each one, ask: did it give me that, or did it just stop the itch?
Most of it is relief from the itch nicotine itself made. Test each one against the beliefs above.

do: Take each line from step 1 and find something that gives you about 80% of it.
Breaks: step outside anyway, without it. Walk, drink water.
Coffee: change the place or the time for the first weeks.
Hands and mouth: gum, a toothpick, seeds.
Vape or pouch at the desk: put mints, sugar-free gum or a cold drink in the same spot.
Stress: ten slow breaths or a two-minute walk before you decide anything.

proof.text: A lab test, not everyday craving: in groups of about 20 smokers paid to stay off, smoking cues pulled harder at day 35 than day 7 on one of three craving scales. Keep the coffee and break swaps past the first month.

ref.cite: Bedi G, Preston KL, Epstein DH, Heishman SJ, Marrone GF, Shaham Y, de Wit H (2011). Incubation of cue-induced cigarette craving during abstinence in human smokers. Biological Psychiatry 69(7):708-11.
ref.quote: Cue-induced craving was greater in Group 3 (35-day) compared with Group 1 (7-day).
ref.note: 86 non-treatment-seeking smokers of 10 or more a day completed, paid $30 a day to stay off for 7, 14 or 35 days. The day 35 vs day 7 contrast is between two of three randomised groups that total 62 (from the reported F(1,59)); it showed on the TCQ-SF Total only, not on QSU-B Factor 1 or 2. Cue craving did not fall on any measure. A lab cue test, not everyday craving.

do: Pick a date a few days to a few weeks out. Write it down and tell one person.
Throw out every pack, vape and pouch the night before.
For three months, nicotine is the one thing. Leave the gym, the diet and the rest of your life as they are.
Treat week 2 as the test: not one puff.
Mark every day you keep. Each one is a complete success, however loud the urge was.
Slipped? Don’t just start again tomorrow. Go back through steps 1–3: what it gave you, which swap was missing, a new date.

proof.text: Without help, most relapses came in the first 8 days of a quit (eight relapse curves from two studies and five untreated groups).

ref.cite: Hughes JR, Keely J, Naud S (2004). Shape of the relapse curve and long-term abstinence among untreated smokers. Addiction 99(1):29-38.
ref.quote: The existing eight relapse curves from two studies of self-quitters and five no-treatment control groups indicate most relapse occurs in the first 8 days.

do: Say “I don’t smoke”, not “I’m trying to quit”.
When the urge comes, name it: “there is a craving”, not “I need one”.
When the urge comes with coffee or a drink, it’s the habit asking, not your body.
Offered one? Answer like a non-smoker: “No thanks, I don’t.” No story, no excuse.
At the old moments (after food, on a break), do what a non-smoker does there: nothing.

proof.text: Of 544 ex-smokers in Australia and the UK, 14 still called themselves smokers trying to quit. A year later 10 of those 14 smoked again, against 7 to 8 in 100 who called themselves ex-smokers or non-smokers.

ref.cite: Callaghan L, Yong HH, Borland R, Cummings KM, Hitchman SC, Fong GT (2021). What kind of smoking identity following quitting would elevate smokers relapse risk? Addictive Behaviors 112:106654.
ref.quote: Participants who described themselves as ‘A smoker trying to quit’ at baseline (Wave 9) had the highest rates of relapse (71.4%) at follow-up survey (Wave 10)
ref.note: 544 former smokers, quit a month or more, in the ITC surveys in Australia (304) and the UK (240), 2013-14; relapse self-reported at 12 months. Table 2: 14 'smoker trying to quit' (71.4% relapsed), 251 ex-smokers (7.2%), 150 non-smokers (8.0%), 126 'smoker who has chosen to no longer smoke' (12.4%); Table 1A prints the ex-smoker and non-smoker counts the other way round (150 and 251) and 129 for the last group. The authors call the first group small. A link, not proof of cause.

do: Help is a tool, not a must. Use it to make the date stick, not to put it off.
Ask a doctor about varenicline.
Or use a patch plus gum or lozenge, not just one.
Still on cigarettes? A vape gets more smokers off them than patches do. Use it as a step, not a stop: put the day you quit the vape on the calendar, within three months.
Quitting a vape? Ask about varenicline too: in two small trials it helped vapers stop.
Put money on it: give a friend a sum to hand back at month 3.

proof.text: In 41 trials (17,395 people), 23 in 100 on varenicline were still off cigarettes at 6 months or more, against 10 in 100 on a dummy pill.

ref.cite: Livingstone-Banks J, Fanshawe TR, Thomas KH, Theodoulou A, Hajizadeh A, Hartman L, Lindson N (2023). Nicotine receptor partial agonists for smoking cessation. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 5:CD006103.
ref.quote: For every 100 people using varenicline to stop smoking, 21 to 25 might successfully stop
ref.note: Summary of findings table 1, abstinence at longest follow-up (6+ months), varenicline vs placebo: 99 per 1000 with placebo, 230 per 1000 (213 to 249) with varenicline; RR 2.32; 41 studies, 17,395 people; high certainty.

gaps.searched: Europe PMC and web searches for the mean or median age when nicotine dependence ended ('age at remission', 'mean age' with remission, recovery, ex-smokers). Read in full: Lopez-Quintero 2011 (NESARC, PMC3227547), Dierker 2008 (NCS-R, PMC2659851), Goodwin 2011 (NESARC, PMC3337717), Chou 2016 (NESARC-III, PMC8154113). Searched again 2026-11-05: web searches for age at quitting or remission among dependent ex-smokers in national US surveys and Australian studies; read Agrawal 2008 (national US survey, PMC2516971).
gaps.why: None reports an average or median age when nicotine dependence ended. Lopez-Quintero gives years from getting hooked to getting free (a median of about 26), not the age. Ages at quitting exist for ex-smokers in general, but those count ordinary smokers, which rule 3 bans in the who-gets-free group. The National Recovery Survey behind the alcohol 'about 38' did not ask about nicotine. Later: our r/stopsmoking harvest could give a self-hooked count of age at quitting from posts that state both age and quit date. The new search found only Agrawal 2008: mean age 40 at quitting among 17,919 people who had smoked 100 cigarettes, ordinary smokers, which rule 3 bans here (listed in notUsed).
gaps.changeNote: Second search added, as the task asked; still no source about people hooked on nicotine, so the kind stays empty.

gaps.searched: Europe PMC and web searches for untreated or unassisted remission among people who had been nicotine-dependent (NESARC, NCS-R, 'natural recovery', 'formal help', 'without treatment'). Read: Lopez-Quintero 2011 (no treatment data), Chou 2016 NESARC-III, Smith 2015 (07). Searched again 2026-11-05: web searches for untreated or unassisted remission among nicotine-dependent people (national US surveys, Australian ex-smoker studies); Alghzawi 2020 (people with severe mental illness who all had help) and Agrawal 2008 checked.
gaps.why: No source counts, among people who were hooked on nicotine and got free, how many never used treatment, a group or medicine. Nearest: Chou 2016 (NESARC-III) found 18.8% of everyone ever hooked had ever used any treatment (27.8% of severe cases), but that counts everyone ever hooked, mild included, not only those who got free, so using it would stretch it. The 07 Australian review (54–69% of ex-smokers quit unassisted) counts ordinary ex-smokers, tag 'users', which kinds.json does not allow here. Later: our r/stopsmoking harvest could count quit posts naming cold turkey against patches, pills or vapes (self-hooked). The Chou 2016 figure now fills quit-status as '81 in 100 had never used any help', because that kind asks exactly that about everyone ever hooked; it still does not count only those who got free, so how-alone stays empty.
gaps.changeNote: Second search added; Chou 2016 moved to quit-status, where it fits without stretching.

gaps.searched: Filled with the owner-liked 07 number (Hughes 2004, 3–5%). Looked for the populations of the studies it pools; the full text is behind a paywall (Wiley returned 403). Looked for a slip-and-when number in a dependent group: West and Hajek 1997 (31 of 101 dependent smokers slipped within 4 weeks, one small trial) and NESARC papers (relapse among ex-smokers in general).
gaps.why: Resolved: kinds.json now allows 'users' for how-slips, so the 3–5% (a v10 number he liked) passes the build with its tag shown. Rule 2 still argues against it, so the number carries a 'propose' note for him to decide.
gaps.changeNote: kinds.json changed after the first review; the open decision moved to the number's 'propose' field.

gaps.searched: 2026-11-05: web search for smokers (dependent or in treatment) who got help early and did better later; looked for a nicotine version of the alcohol '62% vs 43%' (help in the first year).
gaps.why: No study found that compares, among people hooked on nicotine, getting help early against later and counts who was free years on. Nearest: trials where setting a later quit date went with less success, and Kenford 1994 (smoking in week 2 predicts failure), which are about timing a quit, not getting help early.
gaps.changeNote: New gap note: helps-early-help is now picked.

gaps.searched: 2026-11-05: web and PubMed searches for how many people hooked on nicotine get withdrawal when they stop (national US surveys, epidemiologic studies); read Breslau 1992 (PMID 1554030) and Smith 2014 (PMC3935702).
gaps.why: When it peaks is covered by the timeline row (Hughes 2007: worst in week 1, gone by weeks 2–4) and belief 2 (Shiffman 2006: back to normal within 10 days). No fetched source counts how many people hooked on nicotine get withdrawal when they stop. Breslau 1992 says each symptom but two was reported by more than half of 239 young adults who had tried to quit and failed, but they were not checked for addiction and it is per symptom, not per person; Smith 2014 counts withdrawal in current smokers, not in people stopping.
gaps.changeNote: New gap note: how-withdrawal is a new picked kind.

numbers.reason: Share of US 18-to-24-year-olds who vape: ordinary users, a prevalence figure that answers no kind on the menu.
Smokers who want to stop and tried in the past year: ordinary smokers, and no kind on the menu asks it.
Projected share of first-time smokers who get hooked: about how it starts, no kind on the menu.
Teens losing control within days of first inhaling: about how it starts, teens only, no kind on the menu.
Odds of erection problems in smokers: a cost of smoking in ordinary smokers aged 40+, no cost kind on the menu.
Weekly spend of smokers in England: ordinary users; after-first-month does not allow the 'users' tag.
Less sleep in current smokers than never-smokers: ordinary users compared at one night, not a change after quitting; after-sleep is not picked.
Quit ratio among everyone who ever smoked 100 cigarettes: ordinary smokers, which rule 3 bans in the hope group; the counted dependent figure is used instead.
Ex-smokers who quit unassisted (Australia): ordinary ex-smokers, tag 'users', not allowed for how-alone; see the how-alone gap.
Unplanned quit tries lasted longer: no kind on the menu asks planned against unplanned, and it counts ordinary smokers.
Methods smokers used on their last try: what people use, not what works, among current smokers (tag 'users'), which how-abrupt does not allow.
Vapes beat patches or gum for getting off cigarettes: a switch, not an exit; helps-medicine takes the best-tested quit medicine, varenicline.
Varenicline for quitting vaping: 2 small trials, low certainty; helps-medicine takes the 41-trial smoking figure. Candidate for a vape-only line later.
Nicotine replacement against placebo: weaker than varenicline, which fills helps-medicine; one number per kind.

Breslau 1992: each withdrawal symptom but two was reported by more than half of 239 young adults who had tried to quit and failed. Not checked for addiction, per symptom rather than per person; see the how-withdrawal gap.
Agrawal 2008 (national US survey): mean age at quitting among 17,919 people who had smoked 100 cigarettes. Ordinary smokers, which rule 3 bans in who-age.

beliefs.belief: I enjoy it. I don’t want to give it up. → Much of the enjoyment is relief from an itch nicotine gave me. The itch is gone within a month.
beliefs.why: Overlaps the calm row: both say the reward is the itch going quiet. Its proof (withdrawal fades in 2–4 weeks) now answers the “unbearable” row, and its idea lives in plan step 1. Kept in 06-template.json.

beliefs.belief: Smoking keeps my weight down. → A few kilos is a fair trade, and I can handle them.
beliefs.origin: 06-template.json nicotine belief 3 (and 02 research belief “If I quit I’ll balloon.”)
beliefs.why: Five-row limit, and it is about a cost of quitting, not about whether he can quit. The counterpart is a slogan he may not believe. The 4–5 kg figure stays in the timeline (month 3) and fits the after-body number kind.

beliefs.belief: Patches are cheating. Cold turkey or nothing. → I’ll take whatever doubles my chances. Pride doesn’t quit for me.
beliefs.origin: 06-template.json nicotine belief 7 (and 02 research belief “Patches just feed the addiction.”)
beliefs.why: Pushes help as a must, which clashes with his step 5 (help is optional, a tool). Its 3–5% figure counts single unaided attempts, not people: most ex-smokers in Australian studies quit unaided (Smith 2015). The varenicline figure moved to step 5’s proof.
